sections.name: Help: how to use this map
sections.title: Ghana Field Map
sections.abstractText:
Find your place. Tap the round target button (bottom right) to go to where you are, or type the name of your village or town in the search box.

Choose what to see. Open the menu (☰, top left), tap Add layer, choose a folder and tick a map: rain, green plants, wet soil, fires, soil quality, clinics, schools, markets or water points. Under Baselayers you can switch between street map, relief map and satellite photo. Tap a place on the map to see its value or name.

Measure your field. Open the tools (🔧, top right) and choose Measure, choose Area and tap the corners of your field; tap the first corner again to finish. The result is in hectares (ha). 1 ha = 2.47 acres; 1 acre = 0.405 ha.

Coordinates. In the tools (🔧), Coordinates shows the position of a point in GPS coordinates, the Ghana National Grid, UTM and other systems used in Africa.

How to read the maps

Rain – satellite estimate of rain on the latest day; darker colours mean more rain. It covers large areas and can miss a single shower.

How green the plants are (vegetation index) – dark green means many healthy plants, yellow and brown mean few or dry plants. Compare your area with last weeks to see if crops are stressed.

How wet the soil is – computer model of the water in the soil around the roots; good for seeing dry spells over a district, not for a single field.

Fires – fires and hot spots seen by a satellite on the latest day.

Soil maps (SoilGrids, top 5 cm, about 250 m squares) – estimates from a computer model, not a soil test. Acidity: the number is pH × 10, so 55 means pH 5.5. Most crops grow well between pH 6.0 and 7.0 (60–70); below 5.5 (55) the soil is acid. Organic carbon and nitrogen: higher values usually mean more fertile soil. Clay: high values mean heavy soil that holds water; low values mean sandy soil that dries out fast. Ask your agricultural extension officer before you change fertiliser or lime.

Clinics, schools, markets, water points – from OpenStreetMap, a map made by volunteers. Some places are missing, especially water points.

Maps only around the five big cities (Accra, Kumasi, Tamale, Sekondi-Takoradi, Cape Coast) – where rainwater collects, places often under water, land cover, buildings over time, hot and cool places and where people live.

Sources

Map: © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), map service by terrestris. Satellite photo: Sentinel-2 cloudless 2024 by EOX IT Services GmbH (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Rain, plants, soil moisture and fires: NASA EOSDIS GIBS (IMERG, MODIS, SMAP, VIIRS). Soil: ISRIC SoilGrids (CC BY 4.0). Clinics, schools, markets, water points, borders and city maps: Ghana Cities (OpenStreetMap, geoBoundaries, WorldPop, Copernicus, ESA WorldCover, JRC, USGS Landsat). This map is not an official warning service. For weather warnings follow the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet).
